common_name: Tamar Fire Daffodil (Double Yellow and Orange-Red Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Tamar Fire is a Division 4 double daffodil bred by Irish hybridizer Nell Richardson with deep yellow outer segments and orange-red inner segments.

directions: Plant bulbs 5 to 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall. Tamar Fire is a Division 4 (double) daffodil raised by Northern Irish breeder Nell Richardson and registered in 1976, bearing many layers of deep golden-yellow petals shot through with orange-red segments toward the flower's center, giving each bloom a fiery, layered look that holds up well as a cut flower. It carries the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit and has been used as a parent of several later double daffodils. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally after bloom before removing it, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in summer dormancy.

common_name: Pink Pride Daffodil (Tall White Large-Cupped Daffodil with Apricot-Pink Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Pink Pride is a tall Division 2 large-cupped daffodil with a white perianth and a ruffled cup that opens lemon and apricot before deepening to coral-pink.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall. Pink Pride is a Division 2 large-cupped daffodil bred by Dutch hybridizer P.B. van Eeden and registered in 1970, a cross of 'Pink Rim' and 'Lady Kesteven', and was among the first daffodils to show a crown distinctly tinged with pink. Its broad, pure white petals set off a ruffled corona that opens pale lemon-apricot and gradually deepens to coral-pink as the flower ages, especially in cool weather, on stems that reach well over two feet. It increases into large, reliable clumps over the years. Deadhead spent blooms if desired but let the foliage die back naturally to recharge the bulb for next spring.

common_name: Chromacolor Daffodil (White Large-Cupped Daffodil with Bright Pink Corona)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Chromacolor is a Division 2 large-cupped daffodil with broad white petals and a widely flared, bright pink, ruffled corona.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in fall, siting in partial shade where possible since strong, direct sun can bleach out the pink coloring. Chromacolor is a Division 2 (large-cupped) daffodil holding the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, bearing broadly oval white tepals around a widely expanded, ruffled corona in a bright, saturated pink unusual among daffodils. Flowers reach about 4 to 5 inches across and open in mid-spring on sturdy stems roughly a foot and a half tall. Allow foliage to die back fully after bloom before cutting it, since the leaves continue feeding the bulb for next year's pink coloring and flower size.

common_name: Kedron Daffodil (Multi-Flowered Amber-Copper Warm-Climate Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Kedron is a multi-flowered warm-climate daffodil bred by American hybridizer Willis Wheeler, with pale amber-copper to apricot-yellow segments around a disk-shaped deep-orange cup.

directions: Plant bulbs 5 to 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Kedron is a 1974 American hybrid raised by Willis Wheeler, bearing up to two fragrant, amber-copper to apricot-yellow flowers per stem around a flat, disk-shaped, deep orange cup. Unlike many trumpet and large-cup daffodils that need a hard winter chill, Kedron is bred from tazetta and jonquilla stock and perennializes especially well in mild-winter climates such as the Gulf Coast and lower South, where many classic Dutch daffodils fail to return. Let foliage die back naturally after bloom, and divide established clumps only when flowering begins to decline, since Kedron multiplies readily where it is well adapted.

common_name: Petit Four Daffodil (Double White Daffodil with Apricot-and-Pink Center)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Petit Four is a fragrant Division 4 double daffodil with pure white outer petals framing a frilled double cup of peach, ivory, and pink.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Petit Four is a Division 4 (double) daffodil bred by F. Rijnveld and Sons in the Netherlands, registered in 1961 and later honored with the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Merit. Pure white outer petals frame a densely doubled, ruffled center packed with peach, ivory, and lemon-yellow tones that fade toward soft pink as the flower ages, giving each bloom a pastry-like, frosted appearance that explains its name. It is lightly fragrant and blooms in mid-to-late spring. Stake in windy sites since the heavy double flowers can weigh down the stems, and allow foliage to yellow fully before removing it.

common_name: Topolino Daffodil (Dwarf White and Yellow Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Topolino is a dwarf Division 1 trumpet daffodil introduced in 1965, with a cream perianth fading to white around a bright yellow trumpet.

directions: Plant bulbs 4 to 5 inches deep in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade in fall. Topolino is a dwarf Division 1 trumpet daffodil introduced in 1965 and holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, bearing petals that open creamy in bud and fade to near-white around a long, vivid yellow cylindrical trumpet. Standing only 8 to 10 inches tall, it is well suited to rock gardens, the front of borders, and forcing in pots, and it naturalizes reliably, returning and multiplying for years with minimal care. Deadhead if tidiness is wanted, but leave the strappy foliage in place until it yellows naturally to replenish the bulb.

common_name: Candlepower Daffodil (Miniature White Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Candlepower is a miniature Division 1 trumpet daffodil bred by Alec Gray, opening pale yellow-green and maturing to white.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Candlepower is a miniature trumpet-type (Division 1) daffodil bred by renowned English miniature-daffodil specialist Alec Gray, registered in 1975 and included on the American Daffodil Society's approved list of miniature cultivars. Its small, cylindrical trumpet opens pale yellow-green and whitens with age, set within pale perianth segments, on compact stems under 10 inches tall. It is well suited to rock gardens, trough plantings, and the front of borders where larger daffodils would overwhelm its scale. Leave the fine, grass-like foliage to die back naturally, since miniature daffodils in particular rely on a full post-bloom feeding period to rebuild the small bulb.

common_name: Barrii Conspicuus Daffodil (Historic Victorian Small-Cupped Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Barrii Conspicuus (sold today simply as 'Conspicuus') is a Victorian-era Division 3 small-cupped daffodil introduced in 1869, with ruffled creamy-yellow petals around a short, orange-rimmed cup.

directions: Plant bulbs 5 to 6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Barrii Conspicuus, usually sold today under the shorter name 'Conspicuus', was raised by English breeder William Backhouse and introduced in 1869, one of the first short-cupped Barrii-type daffodils to captivate Victorian gardeners; it received the Royal Horticultural Society's First Class Certificate in 1886. Fluttering, creamy-yellow petals surround a short, frilled cup ringed in orange, giving established clumps a butterfly-like effect in mid-spring. It is a vigorous grower that multiplies rapidly with no special care and is still offered by heirloom bulb specialists. Allow foliage to die back fully after bloom, and divide clumps only once flowering begins to decline, since it is content to be left undisturbed for many years.

common_name: Audubon Daffodil (White Large-Cupped Daffodil with Coral-Pink Rim)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Audubon is a Division 2 large-cupped daffodil bred by Grant Mitsch, with pale white petals and a creamy white cup banded in coral pink.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Audubon was bred by respected Pacific Northwest hybridizer Grant Mitsch and registered in 1965, bearing pale white perianth segments around a bowl-shaped cup that is creamy white banded with a broad rim of coral pink. Flowers reach just over 4 inches across and open mid-to-late season on standard-height stems. It is reliably cold-hardy and performs well in naturalized drifts as well as formal beds. Let foliage yellow and collapse naturally after bloom before clearing it away, since premature removal weakens next year's flowering.

common_name: Wee Bee Daffodil (Dwarf Miniature Yellow Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Wee Bee is a dwarf miniature Division 1 trumpet daffodil of pre-1948 Dutch origin, resembling the related miniatures 'Bagatelle' and 'Little Gem'.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Wee Bee is a dwarf miniature trumpet daffodil (Division 1) of pre-1948 Dutch origin, included on the American Daffodil Society's suggested list of miniature-sized daffodils. Its twisted, overlapping yellow perianth segments surround a smooth, slightly constricted trumpet with a deeply notched, flared rim, closely resembling its better-known relatives 'Bagatelle' and 'Little Gem' at a similarly diminutive scale under 5 inches tall. It has also proven a fertile and popular parent in further miniature daffodil breeding. Grow in a rock garden, trough, or raised bed where its small scale will not be lost among larger bulbs, and allow the fine foliage to die back fully after bloom.

common_name: Sun Chariot Daffodil (Bright Yellow Large-Cupped Daffodil with Orange Corona)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Sun Chariot is a Division 2 large-cupped daffodil with bright yellow petals and a short, funnel-shaped orange corona, a multiple award winner from the mid-twentieth century.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Sun Chariot is a Division 2 (large-cupped) daffodil that collected a string of honors through the 1950s and early 1960s, including the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Merit in 1951 and 1963 and awards from the Dutch Royal General Bulb Growers' Association in 1954 and 1956. Bright, clear yellow petals surround a short, funnel-shaped corona in a contrasting warm orange, with flowers reaching roughly 4.5 inches across in early-to-mid season. It remains a dependable, long-lived garden daffodil for mass plantings and borders. Let the foliage die back naturally after bloom to keep the bulb vigorous for the following spring.

common_name: Easter Moon Daffodil (White Large-Cupped Daffodil with Green-Tinged Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Easter Moon is an all-white Division 2 large-cupped daffodil, bred by Wilson before 1954, with a short cup touched with spring-green at the base.

directions: Plant bulbs 5 to 6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall. Easter Moon is a Division 2 (large-cupped) daffodil hybridized by Wilson and in commerce by the early 1950s, bearing solitary, rounded, all-white flowers with a short cup that carries just a touch of spring-green toward its base, fading as the bloom matures. It flowers mid-season on stems in the 12-to-18-inch range and is valued for cutting as well as naturalizing at a wood's edge or under deciduous trees. Allow foliage to die back fully before removing it, since the moon-pale color of the bloom depends on a well-fed bulb each year.

common_name: Canaliculatus Daffodil (Miniature Fragrant Multi-Flowered Tazetta)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Canaliculatus is a miniature tazetta daffodil in commerce since 1915, bearing clusters of four to seven small, fragrant flowers with reflexed white petals and a tiny yellow cup.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade in fall. Canaliculatus is a diminutive tazetta-type daffodil in cultivation since 1915, producing clusters of four to seven small, sweetly fragrant flowers per stem, each with slightly reflexed white petals surrounding a small, flat yellow cup. Standing only about 6 inches tall, it is best suited to warmer climates where tazetta daffodils perennialize most reliably, and it naturalizes readily once established, multiplying into dense clumps over the years. Plant in groups along border fronts, in rock gardens, or in containers where its fragrance can be appreciated up close. Allow foliage to die back naturally, and avoid heavy summer irrigation once the plant goes dormant.

common_name: Maureen Tulip (Tall Marble-White Single Late Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Maureen is a tall 1950 Single Late tulip whose large, oval flowers open pale cream-yellow and mature to glistening marble white.

directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Maureen is a tetraploid Single Late tulip introduced in 1950, among the tallest and most heavily awarded of the classic Dutch tulip cultivars, with very long, sturdy stems carrying large, oval, creamy-white buds that open pale yellow and mature to a glistening marble white. Its height and clean color have made it a long-standing favorite for formal beds, mass border plantings, and cut-flower production, flowering in late spring. As with most tulips, treat as an annual fall-planted display in mild-winter Southern gardens rather than expecting reliable long-term perennializing.

common_name: Red Impression Tulip (Large Ruby-Red Darwin Hybrid Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Red Impression is a sport of Pink Impression with large, glossy ruby-red Darwin Hybrid flowers on sturdy stems.

directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Red Impression is a Darwin Hybrid tulip that arose as a sport of the earlier Pink Impression and was introduced in the early 2000s, producing large, glossy ruby-red blooms up to 6 inches across on thick, wind-resistant stems 20 to 24 inches tall. Like other Darwin Hybrids, it blooms mid-to-late spring and is among the more perennial of tulip classes, capable of returning for several years in climates with cold winters and sharp summer drainage. It is a strong choice for mass landscape plantings and cutting gardens alike.

common_name: Cape Town Tulip (Butter-Yellow Triumph Tulip with Raspberry-Red Edge)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall five to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Cape Town is a modern Triumph tulip with butter-yellow petals edged in raspberry red, the red band widening as the flower ages.

directions: Plant bulbs five to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall. Cape Town is a modern Triumph tulip with butter-yellow petals accented by a raspberry-red edge that widens noticeably as each flower matures and ages in the garden, giving the planting a shifting two-tone effect over its bloom period. Triumph tulips are themselves a cross between early single tulips and single late tulips, prized for their sturdy stems and classic goblet-shaped flowers, and Cape Town blooms in mid-spring at a modest 12 to 16 inches, making it well suited to beds, borders, and containers. Plant in October or November for the best root establishment before winter.

common_name: Super Parrot Tulip (Oversized White Parrot Tulip with Green Feathering)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in a sheltered spot; Super Parrot is a sport of White Dream with large, ruffled white flowers feathered in green on the exterior petals.

directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in a sheltered, full-sun position in fall, since the oversized flowers can be damaged by strong wind or heavy rain. Super Parrot arose as a sport of 'White Dream' and bears extravagantly ruffled and scalloped white blooms with prominent green feathering on the outer petals, resembling the plumage that gives the Parrot tulip group its name. As the large flowers are exposed to sun over several days they open wide and nearly flatten out, revealing their ruffled interior. Blooming in late spring at 16 to 24 inches, Super Parrot pairs well with other late-season bulbs and makes a dramatic cut flower.

common_name: Giuseppe Verdi Tulip (Dwarf Golden-Yellow Kaufmanniana Tulip with Red Markings)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall four to six inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun; Giuseppe Verdi is a dwarf Kaufmanniana tulip named for the composer in 1955, with golden-yellow petals marked red inside and carmine on the reverse.

directions: Plant bulbs four to six inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Giuseppe Verdi is a dwarf Kaufmanniana-group tulip named in 1955 after the Italian composer, bearing large golden-yellow flowers with small red markings on the interior and carmine-red shading toward the base of the exterior petals. Like other Kaufmanniana (waterlily) tulips, its flowers open flat into a star shape during sunny hours and close again at night or in overcast weather, creating two distinct looks from the same bloom. Flowering very early in the season at only 7 to 9 inches tall, it is ideal for rock gardens, raised beds, and containers, and it naturalizes and returns reliably better than many taller hybrid tulip classes.

common_name: Carnaval de Nice Tulip (Fragrant White Double Late Tulip Feathered in Burgundy-Red)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Carnaval de Nice is a fragrant 1953 Double Late tulip with white petals boldly flamed and feathered in burgundy-red, with foliage finely edged in white.

directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Carnaval de Nice is a fragrant Double Late tulip introduced in 1953 and later honored with the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, bearing large, densely packed white blooms boldly streaked and feathered in burgundy-red in a pattern so crisp it looks hand-painted rather than grown naturally. Its grayish-green foliage is finely edged in white, adding interest even before the flowers open. Blooming in late spring around the same time as lilacs and crabapples, it reaches 18 to 20 inches and makes an outstanding, long-lasting cut flower.

common_name: Yalta Crocus (Bicolor Dark Purple and Pale Lavender Hybrid Crocus)

planting.note: Plant corms in fall three to four inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun; Yalta is a large-flowered hybrid between Crocus tommasinianus and Crocus vernus, selected by Latvian bulb breeder Janis Ruksans, with pale lavender outer petals and deep blue-violet inner petals.

directions: Plant corms three to four inches deep in well-drained, average soil in full sun in fall. Yalta is a large-flowered hybrid crocus between Crocus tommasinianus and Crocus vernus selected by noted Latvian bulb breeder Janis Ruksans, producing a distinctive bicolor flower with pale, silvery-lavender outer petals surrounding slightly larger, deep blue-violet inner petals, set off by dark purple stems and bright orange stamens. It flowers very early, often in February into March, ahead of most Dutch crocus, and multiplies readily once established. Plant in generous drifts in a lawn, rock garden, or border front where its early color is welcome, and allow foliage to die back naturally before mowing over naturalized plantings.

common_name: Galatea Snowdrop (Vigorous Historic Long-Pedicelled Snowdrop)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Galatea is a vigorous nineteenth-century hybrid snowdrop with a notably long flower stalk, though less exaggerated than that of the related 'Magnet'.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, ideally beneath deciduous trees where bulbs get good light before the canopy leafs out. Galatea is an old hybrid snowdrop dating from the end of the 19th century, bearing rounded white flowers held on a long pedicel, a trait it shares with (though less pronounced than) its well-known relative 'Magnet'. It clumps up readily and is valued among snowdrop growers for its reliable vigor in ordinary garden conditions, including at the back of borders among later-flowering perennials. Divide and transplant clumps while still in leaf ('in the green'), just after flowering, for the most reliable results, and purchase only nursery-propagated bulbs.

common_name: Green Tear Snowdrop (Dark Green-Marked Dutch Snowdrop)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Green Tear was found by Gert-Jan van der Kolk near Zutphen in the Netherlands in 2000, with unusually dark green markings on both the outer and inner petals.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Green Tear was discovered in a wild population of common snowdrop near Zutphen in the Netherlands in 2000 by Gert-Jan van der Kolk, and stands out among green-marked snowdrops for unusually dark, strongly lined green markings on both the outer and inner segments; the inner segments can appear almost entirely green but for a narrow white border at the tip. It is an early-flowering, tall, and robust cultivar, typically carrying two flowers per stem. Divide and transplant clumps while still in leaf immediately after flowering for best results, and source bulbs only from reputable nursery propagation, never wild-collected stock.

common_name: Green Mile Snowdrop (Belgian Green-Marked Hybrid Snowdrop)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Green Mile was found in Belgium by breeder Robin Callens and is prized among collectors for its distinctive green patterning, set apart from similarly marked cultivars such as 'Green Tear'.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Green Mile is a sought-after Belgian-raised snowdrop found by breeder Robin Callens, valued by collectors for its distinctive green markings, which differ in pattern and tone from similarly green-marked cultivars such as 'Green Tear', making side-by-side comparison a favorite pastime among dedicated galanthophiles. As with other green-marked snowdrops, flowering is in late winter into early spring on compact stems. Divide and transplant clumps while still in leaf immediately after flowering for the most reliable establishment, and buy only nursery-propagated bulbs from a reputable specialty source given the premium placed on named snowdrop cultivars.
sources: Scottish Rock Garden Club forum records

common_name: Jenny Robinson Grape Hyacinth (Pale Powder-Blue Muscari)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall three inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun; Jenny Robinson was found in Cyprus by National Collection holder Jenny Robinson and bears closely packed spikes of pale, powder-blue flowers shading to white at the top.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Jenny Robinson, also offered under the synonym 'Baby's Breath', was found growing in Cyprus by one-time National Collection holder Jenny Robinson, for whom it was later named, and carries the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. It bears closely packed, sweetly scented spikes of pale powder-blue florets that shade to white toward the tip of the spike, a softer look than the more common deep-blue grape hyacinths. It clumps well without becoming invasive, unlike some common Muscari species, and is a good choice for the front of borders or rock gardens. Let foliage die back naturally after bloom before clearing it away.

common_name: Grape Ice Grape Hyacinth (Tricolor Blue-to-White Muscari)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall three to four inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Grape Ice shows a striking tricolor effect, with dark violet-purple florets at the base of the spike shading through paler lilac to bright white at the top.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Grape Ice is a selection of broadleaf grape hyacinth prized for its striking tricolor flower spike: florets at the base open a dark violet-purple, those in the middle lighten to a paler lilac, and the uppermost sterile florets open bright white, giving each spike a frosted, two-tone look reminiscent of its name. It is lightly scented, deer resistant, and performs well both naturalized in the garden and forced indoors in pots for early bloom. Each plant typically produces a single broad leaf, distinguishing it from the narrower, grassier foliage of common grape hyacinth. Allow foliage to die back fully before removing it.

common_name: Fondant Hyacinth (Apple-Blossom Pink Fragrant Hyacinth)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Fondant, also sold as 'Pink Frosting', bears densely packed, bell-shaped flower spikes in dainty apple-blossom pink softening to pale blush at the petal edges.

directions: Plant bulbs 4 to 6 inches deep in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Fondant, marketed in some catalogs under the name 'Pink Frosting', was hybridized in 1983 and has since collected numerous horticultural awards for its densely packed, bell-shaped flower spikes in a soft apple-blossom pink that pales to a gentle blush at the petal edges, carrying the classic intense, honeyed hyacinth fragrance. It reaches about a foot tall and pairs well in formal beds or containers with other pastel spring bulbs. For indoor forcing, chill bulbs in the dark near 40 degrees Fahrenheit for ten to twelve weeks before bringing them into warmth and light.

common_name: Saturnus Checkered Lily (Bright Reddish-Violet Checkered Fritillary)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall three to four inches deep in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Saturnus is one of the brightest-colored selections of checkered lily, with strongly checkered reddish-violet and purplish-pink bell-shaped flowers.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, in a spot that stays damp through spring but is not waterlogged. Saturnus is regarded as one of the brightest-colored selections of checkered lily, bearing singular or paired, broadly bell-shaped, pendant flowers in a vivid reddish-violet strongly checkered with purplish-pink, each up to 1.75 inches long, atop slender stems clothed in narrow, grey-green leaves. Like other checkered lily forms it is well suited to naturalizing in damp meadow grass or at the edge of a pond or bog garden, where it can seed and spread gradually over time. Allow foliage to die back fully after bloom before mowing over naturalized plantings.

common_name: Lutea Maxima Crown Imperial (Large Deep Yellow Crown Imperial)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in deep, rich, well-drained alkaline soil in full sun; Lutea Maxima, also sold as 'Maxima Lutea', bears deep yellow, bell-shaped flowers beneath a topknot of leaves atop stout three- to four-foot stems, in cultivation since 1857.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 to 8 inches deep in deep, rich, well-drained, alkaline-leaning soil in a warm, full-sun position in fall, choosing a spot where the bulbs can be left undisturbed for years. Lutea Maxima, sometimes sold under the reversed name 'Maxima Lutea', has been grown in gardens since 1857 and carries the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, producing stout, erect stems up to 4 feet tall topped by a whorl of leaves above a ring of six or more large, nodding, bright yellow bell-shaped flowers in mid-to-late spring, giving the whole plant a pineapple-like silhouette. Like other crown imperials, its bulbs give off a musky, skunk-like odor that helps deter deer and rodents from the garden. Avoid disturbing the bulbs once planted, and do not let them sit in winter-wet soil, which quickly causes rot.

common_name: Lucy Ball Allium (Fragrant Bright Purple Giant Ornamental Onion)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun; Lucy Ball is a fragrant hybrid of Allium hollandicum and Allium macleanii bred by Dutch plant breeder Jan Bijl, with bright purple flower spheres on stems up to four feet tall.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 to 8 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun in fall, choosing a site with sharp winter drainage since standing moisture rots the large bulbs. Lucy Ball is a hybrid of Allium hollandicum and Allium macleanii bred by noted Dutch plant breeder Jan Bijl, producing fragrant, tightly packed, bright purple flower spheres 5 to 6 inches across held well above strap-like basal foliage on sturdy stems that can top 4 feet. It is a comparatively rarely offered allium cultivar, flowering in early summer and valued both for cutting and for its pollinator appeal. The pungent bulbs, leaves, and stems are naturally unpalatable to deer and rodents, making it a reliable choice in gardens troubled by browsing wildlife.

common_name: Round and Purple Allium (Giant Lavender-Purple Ornamental Onion)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun; Round and Purple produces some of the largest flower heads among ornamental onions, star-shaped lavender-purple florets forming a globe up to 6 inches across on stems to 3 feet.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 to 8 inches deep in rich, sandy to gritty, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Round and Purple is valued for having some of the largest flower heads in the ornamental onion group, producing dense, globe-shaped clusters of star-shaped lavender-purple florets up to 6 inches across on strong stems reaching about 3 feet, blooming from late spring into early summer. The flower heads remain ornamental well into summer even as they fade and dry, making them useful for both fresh and dried arrangements. It naturalizes readily and returns reliably year after year, and like other alliums is generally left alone by deer while attracting bees, butterflies, and other pollinators. Plant bulbs in groups of ten or more for the strongest visual impact.
